opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to start with what VLA models actually do well and where they hit a ceiling. A vision-language-action model takes the huge amount of knowledge in a pretrained vision-language model, its understanding of objects, of instructions, of common sense, and maps it more or less directly to motor commands. That's been a big step forward. You can tell a robot "put the apple in the bowl" and it generalizes to objects and scenes it has never seen, which was very hard five years ago.

But the core of a VLA is still a reactive policy. It looks at the current observation and outputs the next action. It doesn't really have an internal sense of what will happen if it does that action. Physics, contact, how a cloth will fold, whether a stack will topple, it learns these only implicitly, from whatever demonstrations it happened to see. That's the bottleneck. Robot data is expensive. Every teleoperated demonstration costs human time, and you will never collect enough to cover the long tail of the physical world.

A world model changes the question. Instead of asking "what action should I take?", the model learns "if I take this action, what will the world look like next?" Once you have that, a few things open up.

First, data. Predicting the future is something you can learn from video at enormous scale: human videos, YouTube, any footage of things moving and interacting, without action labels. That's orders of magnitude more data than robot demonstrations. The model can absorb intuitive physics from the whole visual record of the world, and then you only need a relatively small amount of robot data to ground it to your specific body.

Second, planning and reasoning. If the robot can imagine the consequences of its actions, it can try things out in its head before committing in the real world. That's much closer to how people operate. When you reach for a full cup of coffee, you're implicitly simulating how it will slosh. That kind of lookahead is what lets you handle new, long-horizon tasks instead of just pattern-matching on what you've seen before.

Third, the world model can serve as a learned simulator. In robotics we've relied heavily on physics simulators for training, and they've been great for locomotion, but they struggle with deformable objects, fluids, and visual realism. A world model learned from real data could become a simulator that's realistic by construction, where you can run reinforcement learning, evaluate policies, and generate synthetic training data far more cheaply than in the real world.

I don't see this as world models replacing VLAs outright. More likely they merge: the language and semantic understanding of a VLM, plus a predictive model of physics and dynamics, plus an action head. But I do think the center of gravity shifts from imitating actions toward understanding and predicting the world. Imitation gets you to competence on familiar tasks. Prediction is what gets you to robustness and real generalization, and that's ultimately what we need for robots to work in homes and other unstructured environments.

There are still hard open problems. Predictions drift over long horizons, it's expensive to generate video-level predictions fast enough for real-time control, and it's unclear what the right representation is, whether pixels, latent features, or something more abstract. But directionally, I think that's where the next big leap comes from.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about why world models might be the next paradigm, I start with what VLA, vision-language-action, actually does and where it hits a ceiling.

VLA is essentially a very powerful imitation learner. You take a pretrained vision-language backbone, you feed it human teleoperation data, and you train it to map what the robot sees and what you tell it into actions. That has worked remarkably well. The models generalize across objects, across language instructions, across scenes in ways that would have seemed like science fiction five years ago. But it is still fundamentally bottlenecked on human demonstration data. Every new skill, every new embodiment, you need people with controllers collecting trajectories. And robot data is not like internet text. It does not exist in the wild. It is slow and expensive to produce, and no matter how many data collection teams you hire, you are orders of magnitude away from the scale that made language models work.

The second limitation is that a VLA has no explicit notion of consequences. It learned "in this situation, humans tended to do this." It did not learn "if I push here, the cup will tip." So when it fails, it fails somewhat blindly. It cannot look ahead, it cannot ask what would happen if I tried something else, it cannot recover gracefully from a state it has never seen in the demonstrations.

A world model attacks both problems at once. The idea is to learn a model of how the world evolves: given the current observation and an action, predict what you will see next. The beautiful thing is that this objective does not require action labels from experts. You can train on passive video, on failed robot trials, on humans doing things with their hands, on simulation. Suddenly the data pool is not "demonstrations we collected" but "all the video of the physical world that exists," which is enormous. That is the scaling story that VLA lacks.

And once you have a model that can predict the future, robot behavior changes qualitatively. You can plan. You can imagine ten different ways of grasping something, roll them forward in the model, and pick the one that works. You can do reinforcement learning inside the imagined world, so the robot practices millions of times without wearing out hardware or breaking things. You can generate synthetic training data for policies. The world model becomes a kind of mental sandbox, which is really what we think humans and animals do. We do not just react, we simulate.

I want to be honest that this is still speculative. The video prediction models today are impressive visually but often physically wrong in subtle ways, and robots are very sensitive to subtle physical wrongness. Long-horizon prediction compounds errors. Latency and compute are real issues if you want to plan in the loop at control frequency. So I would not say world models replace VLA tomorrow. More likely we see a convergence, where the action model and the predictive model become parts of one system, with the world model giving it the physical understanding and planning ability that pure imitation cannot.

But if you ask what gets us from robots that are good at narrow demonstrated tasks to robots that genuinely understand their environment and adapt, I think learning to predict the world is the most promising path I see.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between learning what action to take and learning what happens when you take an action. A vision-language-action model maps what the robot sees, together with an instruction, into an action. That’s a powerful approach. But a world model tries to predict how the environment will change as the robot acts.

If that prediction is sufficiently accurate, the robot can consider different actions before executing them. If I push this object, will it slide or fall? If I move the gripper this way, will I collide with something? You can use those predictions for planning, and potentially for training policies with less physical interaction.

That’s particularly attractive in robotics because collecting real-world experience is expensive. But the challenge is that a visually plausible prediction isn’t necessarily a physically accurate one. Small errors in contact or motion can completely change whether a task succeeds, and those errors accumulate over longer predictions.

So I see world models as a possible next paradigm because they could make prediction and planning central to robot behavior. I wouldn’t necessarily say they replace vision-language-action models. A policy could propose actions, and a world model could help evaluate and refine them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think world models offer a way to move from reacting to observations to reasoning about consequences. A vision-language-action model maps what the robot sees and what you ask it to do into actions. That’s powerful, but the prediction of what happens next is often implicit. A world model tries to make that explicit: if I take this action, how will the environment change?

Once you have that capability, the robot can imagine different action sequences, compare their outcomes, and choose a promising one before executing it. It can also replan when the real outcome differs from its prediction. That could be particularly valuable for tasks that require many steps or involve unfamiliar situations.

The challenge is that a model can generate something that looks plausible while getting the physics wrong. For robotics, those details matter—whether an object slips, whether contact happens, whether an action actually succeeds. So I see world models as a possible next paradigm, but not necessarily as a replacement for action models. The two could work together: an action model proposes what to do, and a world model helps evaluate the consequences.
